text.p: French bank Credit Lyonnais, which reported on Thursday that 1996 net attributable profit of 202 million francs, up from 13 billion francs the previous year, gave the following details on its performance.

The state-controlled bank said net banking income rose to 44.5 billion francs from 43.4 billion, but was up 5.9 percent on a constant consolidation basis, thanks to buoyant international and capital markets activities.
Net fee income was up 7.9 percent relative to 1995 at 11.8 billion and up 13 percent on a constant consolidation basis.
This change reflected growth in financial services and robust performances in marketing of life and non-insurance products.
Aggregate fee income accounted for 31.7 percent of total banking income in 1996. Operating income rose 42 percent to 9.5 billion francs and 35 percent on a like-for-like basis.

It said operating expenses were kept under control as a result of the group's restructuring drive -- personnel costs were down one percent on a constant consolidation basis after staff cuts in France. The efficiency ratio improved a sharp six points, falling to less than 79 percent.
Operating provisions net of recovery totalled 5.7 billion francs, down 2.1 percent relative to the previous year.
As a result, pretax pre-exceptional income, including the group's share in results of companies accounted for under the equity method, increased to 4.5 billion from 1.5 billion.
"This result reflects the recovery achieved across the group's businesses," it said.

All four profit centres posted better results. In France, net profit before tax picked up strongly, despite reduced return on customer lending resulting from lower interest rates and tough competition.

The improvement stemmed partly from a 3.5 percent decline in operating expenses and partly from a fall in the cost of risk. The asset management sector boosted funds under management by 13 percent to 452 billion francs.
In Europe, the situation improved on a like-for-like basis with operating income rising 34 percent and allocations to provisions down 20 percent, reflecting cleaner loan portfolios.
In the rest of the world, the commercial banking sector posted a 60 percent rise in operating profit, reflecting healthy performances in all geographic areas.

Capital market activities multiplied their operating income on a constant consolidation basis by 2.5 times, owing to a rise in total banking income, up 29 percent, compared with a slower rise in operating expenses and depreciation, up 10 percent.

Net additions to provisions on individual doubtful loans were down 25 percent, cutting the cost of risk, despite further heavy provisions on small and medium size businesses. The provisioning ratio on doubtful loans was 64.4 percent, compared with 62.5 percent in 1995. Coverage of sensitive real estate exposure increased to 66.5 percent from 58.5 percent.
Coverage of sovereign risks rose to 58 percent from 54 percent.

Exceptional provisions of 1.87 billion were made for restructuring in France. There was a further 607 million in provisions for the rest of Europe, along with a 200 million charge for altering computer systems to cope with the initial phase of European monetary union.

Net profit came to 1.49 billion francs after a provision of 107 million francs for payment to the state under the return to better fortune clause. Minority interests in net profit totalled 1.28 billion francs. Group share of net profit was 309 million francs and 202 million francs after the 107 million franc provision for payment to the state.

Group net assets including minority interests and the reserve for general banking risks totalled 44.42 billion francs compared with 42.1 billion. The international solvency ratio at end 1996 was 8.7 percent with a tier one ratio of 4.56 percent compared with 4.47 percent in 1995. Net book value per share was 490.80 francs compared with 465.50 francs.
